title: Six: The Weight of Still Water

blocks.c: Six: The Weight of Still Water
The gates closed on the first of October at eleven in the morning, and nothing happened, and everybody went home.

That is the thing nobody photographs. A dam does not fill a valley the way a bath fills; the Ashlie in October carried perhaps thirty million gallons a day and the reservoir was designed to hold eleven thousand million, and when the gates came down the river simply stopped going through the wall and began, very quietly, to spread out over the flat ground behind it at the rate of about a foot a week.
Ilse stood on the temporary bridge with Cordell and four of his men and watched a river not go somewhere.
"That's it?"
"That's it. It's the least dramatic thing in engineering." He handed her a thermos cup. "Come back at Christmas."
The first of October

There were eleven people on the bridge and four of them were photographers from the county papers, and there was no ceremony, because the Board had considered a ceremony and the Board's public relations man had concluded, correctly, that there is no way to hold one.
Cordell had asked her, in September, whether she wanted to be there.
"Is it usual for the archivist to attend?"
"There is no usual. You are the fourth archivist I have met and the other three were on the telephone."

So she went, and stood at the rail, and at eleven o'clock two men in a control cabin the size of a shed did something with a panel, and eleven hundred tons of steel came down at a rate of four feet a minute, and the noise it made was much less than she had expected and went on for much longer.

Below the dam the river ran on for a while out of the pipework, thinning, and then it was a trickle over gravel, and there were four men from the fisheries board down there in waders taking trout out of the pools by hand and putting them in tanks, and that, oddly, was the thing that made her put her hand over her mouth: not the gate, but four men in a dry riverbed in October catching fish in their hands so that they could be carried somewhere else.
Emrys Pike did not come. She had not expected him to and had asked anyway, on the twenty-eighth, and he had said, without heat: "I've watched enough of it from the inside."

At about a quarter past eleven the photographers left. By noon the whole site had gone back to work, because a gate closing is not a milestone in the construction programme; the milestone had been three weeks earlier, when the grouting was signed off, and the men had marked that one in the site hut with a crate of beer.
Ilse stayed until two, walking the shoreline that did not exist yet, watching the flat green floor of a valley begin, invisibly, to become the bottom of something.
The last three weeks
She had three weeks left on the commission and she spent them on the deposit, which is the unglamorous end of the work and the only part that lasts.

Everything she had recovered went to the county Record Office in ninety-one boxes: the parish chest entire; the school records; the Stammers negatives, nine hundred plates, repacked in acid-free sleeves at her own expense because the estimate had not run to it; the shop ledger; the chapel minute book; the beekeeper's ledger of a man who had kept eleven stocks for forty years, which Emrys Pike gave her in September and which she accepted after arguing with him for an hour about whether it was a public record, and which is now the most requested single item in the Hallowmere collection because it turns out that people want to read about bees.

She wrote the finding aid herself, which is unusual for a deposit that size, and it took her the whole of October and eleven days into November past the end of her contract, unpaid, in a room in the county town.

A finding aid is a catalogue. It is a description of every item in a collection, arranged by the structure of the original records rather than by subject, with a general introduction describing what the collection is, where it came from, how it came to be as it is, and what is not in it.
That last part is the part that mattered.
The introduction

She wrote eleven drafts of the introductory note to the Hallowmere collection. The tenth was seven pages long and contained everything: Mrs. Sowerby's interview in full, the Medical Officer's figures, the fee book, the death register, the two names, her mother.

She read it through on a Tuesday evening in November and understood that it was a work of history and not a work of cataloguing, and that she had written it because she wanted to be the person who found it, and that this was a perfectly natural and entirely disqualifying reason to put something in a finding aid.
She threw it away and wrote the eleventh draft in ninety minutes, and it is what stands at the front of the collection today.
Hallowmere parish and school records, 1561-1994. 91 boxes.

The parish of Hallowmere was inundated in 1994-95 on the completion of the Ashlie reservoir. The records described here were recovered from the parish chest, the school, the chapel and private hands between April and September 1994 under a commission from the Northern Water Board.
Users should note the following.

1. The burial register (HAL/P/11) records five child burials between 12 and 22 February 1942. The county Medical Officer's annual report for 1942 (CC/MOH/68) records three deaths at Hallowmere in that outbreak, and the register of deaths for the sub-district records three. The burial fee book (HAL/P/19) records payment for three graves. The churchyard plan (HAL/P/23) and the monumental survey made in 1994 (HAL/S/1-4) locate three graves of 1942, of which two are marked with initials only.
2. The school admission register (HAL/E/2) records 39 evacuated children admitted in September 1940. The attendance register (HAL/E/4) and the school log book (HAL/E/1) record 41.

3. These inconsistencies are not errors of transcription and have been checked against the originals. The compiler has formed a view as to their explanation. That view is set out in a statement deposited with this collection as HAL/X/1, together with the evidence for it, including a record of interview made in June 1994 with a surviving witness. HAL/X/1 is closed to public inspection until 1 January 2025 and thereafter is open without restriction.
4. The compiler was personally connected to the events described in HAL/X/1 and has recorded the nature of that connection within it.
Four numbered paragraphs. No story at all.
She was extremely pleased with it and could not explain to a single person in her life why.
HAL/X/1
The statement runs to forty-one pages and she wrote it in December, in her own flat, with the tin of photographs on the table.

It contains everything: the documents, in order, with references; the interview, in full, written up the same day, with a note of what was said off the record and why she considered it on; her own connection, stated plainly in the third paragraph and not mentioned again; and the account Emrys Pike gave her over four evenings in September, in his own words, read back to him and signed by him on the last day of the month in the presence of Hollis Cordell, who witnessed it and who has never spoken about it to anybody.
At the end of it, she wrote four paragraphs of her own, which are the only opinion in ninety-one boxes.
The compiler makes the following observations, which are opinion and are marked as such.

The events of February 1942 involved the making of false entries in a parish register by a clerk in holy orders, and the concealment from a local authority of two children in its care, and were criminal at the time. No prosecution was ever brought because nobody outside the parish ever knew, and everybody inside it did.

Five adults are named as having been present at the vestry meeting of 19 February 1942. Four are dead. The fifth was ninety-five at the date of interview and had waited fifty-two years to be asked. Two children were preserved together who would otherwise have been separated by an authority acting lawfully and with no ill intent. Both lived ordinary lives. One left the valley and never returned. One never left it.

It is not the function of an archivist to approve or condemn what is in the records. It is the function of an archivist to ensure that the record cannot be quietly disposed of, and that what was written down can be checked against what else was written down. Everything necessary to check this account is in this collection and is listed in the schedule at page 39.

The compiler notes that the arrangement of February 1942 was held for fifty-two years by an entire community and was undone in eleven weeks by one person reading a fee book. Communities are not good at keeping secrets. They are good at not being asked.
Christmas
She went back at Christmas, as Cordell had told her to.

The road down into the valley was gone — closed at the gate, and beyond the gate the tarmac ran forty yards and stopped at a shoreline. She stood at the end of a road she had driven down every day for six months and looked at the water.

The valley floor was under. All of it. The green, the beech avenue, the lane past the mill, the hard-standing behind the village hall where a caravan had stood: all of it under eleven feet of very still, very cold, brown-grey water, and the surface of it perfectly flat in the windless afternoon, with a heron standing in what had been somebody's garden.
Above the water, the church tower.

They had left it, in the end; the diocese and the Board had argued for two years and the tower had won, because it was fifteenth century and because at full supply level it would stand eleven feet clear and be, as the Board's own report put it, an amenity.

Ilse Vanterpool stood at the end of the road in the cold and looked at a tower coming out of a lake, and Cordell had been right: she got it all at once, and it was not sadness, exactly. It was a physical understanding of weight. There were eleven feet of water where she had walked, and by spring there would be ninety, and water is heavy, and it does not move, and it does not care, and there is a great deal of it.
She stood there for about an hour.

Then she drove up to Culverton, because it was on the way, and walked through a new churchyard with two hundred and six stones set in four straight rows in a field with a wire fence round it, and found, in the third row, near the end, a small sandstone headstone with M.R. and 1942 cut on it by hand, and beside it its twin.
They had been set up level, and the mason had packed them with the same stone as the rest, so that the different-coloured packing was gone.
There was no lichen on the lower south face of either of them. It takes decades. It will come.
The photographs
There was one decision left and she made it in the week between Christmas and the new year, sitting on the floor of her flat with the biscuit tin.
Forty-one contact prints. On the back of each, in pencil, in the hand of a blacksmith who took photographs: a date and the names of everyone in the frame.

An archivist knows what to do with such an object and Ilse did it: she listed it, item by item, and described the tin, and noted the provenance in a single sentence — Given to the compiler by E. Pike, Ford Cottage, Hallowmere, 8 July 1994; stated by him to have been given to him by A. Stammers, 1961 — and prepared it for deposit with the rest of the Stammers material, where it belongs, because a photographer's work should stay together and because those forty-one prints are the only surviving photographs of the interior of a school that no longer exists.
Then she took one of them out.

She sat with it on the floor for a long time: a girl of nine at the front on the left, chin up, hands behind her back, in a room with a piano and a paper chain and thirty-nine other children, four months into being an orphan and eighteen months out from being somebody else.

There is a rule about this and Ilse had enforced it against other people for fourteen years. You do not break a collection. You do not take one item out because you have a personal interest in it; that is precisely how collections are destroyed, one reasonable exception at a time, and every archivist has stood in a strong room holding a folder with a gap in it and cursed a dead man who thought his reason was good.
She put it back in the tin.

Then she photographed it, twice, properly, with a copy stand borrowed from work, and had a print made, and put the print in a frame, and hung it in her hall, and wrote a note for the file recording that she had done so and that the original was deposited entire.
It is, she thought, the whole difference: the record goes to the strong room, and you may keep a copy, and you must say that you have.
Ford Cottage, at Culverton

He had four acres and a bungalow and the eleven hives were in a row facing south-east against a hedge, and he had put the stands out in the same order and the same spacing, which she noticed and did not remark on.
"You found the graves, then."
"Third row."

"Aye. I'll get up there Sundays. It's a bus and a walk." He put the kettle on. "The girl of twenty-five got the declaration through in November. I'm on the pension. There's a card with my name on it in my coat and I have took it out and looked at it, I should think, forty times."
"Which name?"
Emrys Pike put two mugs on the table.

"That's the thing," he said. "I told them. I sat in that solicitor's office in the town with a woman I'd never met and I told her the whole of it, everything, the vestry and the register and the stones, and I waited to be arrested, and she wrote it down and she said: right, Mr. Pike, so the position is that you have been known as Emrys Pike since 1942, and that is your name, because a name is what you are known by and always has been, and the rest is a matter of birth records which we can note as unavailable."
"That's the law," said Ilse. "That is, genuinely, the law."
"Fifty-two years," he said.
They drank the tea.
"Miss Vanterpool. What did you do with it? In the end. The record."
She had prepared four different answers on the drive and used none of them.

"It's all deposited," she said. "The documents are catalogued and open, and anybody can go and look at them tomorrow, and the introduction to the collection says in four numbered paragraphs that they contradict each other and where the contradictions are. And the explanation — Mrs. Sowerby, your statement, my mother, all of it — is in one sealed file that nobody may read until 2025."

"Because it's thirty years, and thirty years is the standard closure for a record affecting a living person, and because you will be ninety-six." She turned the mug round. "It is not a secret, Mr. Pike. That is the part I need you to understand, because I have thought about very little else since August. If I had left it out, it would have been a secret, and secrets die with the last person who knows them, and then somebody in 2080 finds a burial register that doesn't match a Medical Officer's report and there is nobody alive to explain it and the true version is gone for good."
"And this way?"

"This way it is a record with a date on it. It exists. It is listed. It is in the catalogue where anybody can see that it is there and that they cannot read it yet. And on the first of January 2025 a person I will probably never meet will order up a box at table four and find forty-one pages and a tin of photographs, and every single thing in it will be checkable against something else in the same collection." She looked up. "That is the entire difference between a record and a rumour, and it is the only thing my profession is for."
Emrys Pike considered this for a while.
"Anwen Prosser would have liked you," he said. "She'd have argued with you for four hours and then she'd have liked you."
The last thing
He walked her out to the car at the end of the afternoon, past the hives, which were quiet, it being December, and doing what bees do in December, which is to sit in a ball in the dark and eat.
"They're alive in there?"

"Every one. They'll not come out till February and there's nothing you can do for them and nothing you can know. You feed them in September and then you wait five months." He put his hand flat on the roof of the nearest hive, the way another man would put a hand on a gate. "That's the job. Most of the job is not knowing and not opening it to look."
"That sounds like a reproach."

"It's not." He almost smiled. "You opened it. It wanted opening. It's just that I've had fifty-two years of the other and I'd not like you to think I was ashamed of them all, because I was not, not one of them. They did a wicked thing in a vestry on a Thursday and it was the right thing and they never once discussed it again, in fifty-two years, not one of them, not even at a funeral. Do you know what that is?"
"No."
"It's love," said Emrys Pike. "It's just love done by farmers."
She drove back down the hill in the dark, and stopped at the top of the rise where you can see the whole of the reservoir, and got out.

There was a moon. The water was absolutely still, eleven miles of it, and it held the moon and the shoulder of the hill and one small hard shape near the middle which was a tower with nothing under it that anybody could see.

Ilse Vanterpool stood on a road in the cold with a car door open behind her and thought about ninety-one boxes in a strong room forty miles away, catalogued, listed, referenced, on a shelf with a number, where they would sit in the dark and be quiet and not go anywhere, and be there on the first of January 2025, and on the first of January 2125, if anyone had done their job.
Then she got back in the car, because it was cold, and because the record was made, and because there was nothing else that needed doing.

End of the sample series. All six chapters are original prose written for the Offline Reader repository — the parish, the valley, the reservoir and every document quoted are invented. Nothing here was fetched from anywhere, which is why it opens with the network off.
